hints: Use the electrical-power relationship that contains the given power and potential difference.
Rearrange P = VI to make I the subject before substituting the values.
walkthrough: For the resistance wire, P = VI.
Rearrange to I = P / V.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the electrical-power relationship P = VI.
Calculates the current as 4.5 A from 36 / 8.0.

hints: Use the current from part (i) to determine the charge passing through the wire in 50 s.
Then divide the total charge by the magnitude of the charge on one electron.
walkthrough: From part (i), the current is I = 4.5 A.
The charge passing in 50 s is Q = It = 4.5 × 50 = 225 C.
For electrons, Q = Ne, so N = Q / e = 225 / (1.6 × 10^-19).
N = 1.4 × 10^21 free electrons.

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates the charge passed as 225 C from Q = It = 4.5 × 50.
Uses N = Q / e to obtain 1.4 × 10^21 electrons.

hints: Use a power relationship that contains the known potential difference and power, or use the current found in part (i).
Rearrange P = V^2 / R, P = I^2R, or V = IR to make R the subject.
walkthrough: Use P = V^2 / R, so R = V^2 / P.
The resistance of the wire is 1.8 Ω.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses R = V^2 / P, R = V / I, R = P / I^2, or an equivalent valid resistance relationship.

hints: Use the resistance from part (a)(iii) and convert the cross-sectional area from mm^2 to m^2.
Rearrange R = ρL / A to make the wire length L the subject.
walkthrough: From part (a)(iii), R = 1.8 Ω, and the area is A = 0.25 mm^2 = 0.25 × 10^-6 m^2.
Rearrange R = ρL / A to L = RA / ρ.
The wire length is 0.32 m.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses R = ρL / A and rearranges it to determine L.
Uses the converted area and obtains a wire length of 0.32 m.

hints: Compare the cross-sectional areas first; the wires have the same material and length.
Then use the fixed battery potential difference to relate the resistance change to current and power.
walkthrough: The second wire has a greater diameter, so it has a greater cross-sectional area.
With the same resistivity and length, R = ρL / A shows that the second wire has less resistance.
The potential difference across the wire remains 8.0 V, so the lower resistance gives a greater current.
Since P = VI, the second wire dissipates more power.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that the greater diameter gives a greater cross-sectional area and hence less resistance for the same material and length.
States that the same potential difference gives a greater current and therefore more power dissipated.

hints: Compare the potential difference across the original resistance wire before and after the second identical ideal battery is connected in parallel.
With the wire resistance unchanged, use the unchanged potential difference to decide what happens to the wire current and power.
walkthrough: Each ideal battery has an e.m.f. of 8.0 V, so connecting the second one in parallel does not change the 8.0 V potential difference across the original resistance wire.
The resistance of the original wire is unchanged, so its current remains the same.
Since both the current and potential difference across the wire are unchanged, P = VI shows that the power dissipated by the original wire stays the same.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the current in the original resistance wire is unchanged.
Explains that the potential difference across the wire is unchanged and hence the power stays the same.
